threads_text: Musk says SpaceX just closed $40 billion in debt to buy NVIDIA GPUs that arrive in 2027. In the same breath he said lenders have stopped funding most AI cloud startups and that 200+ of them face death and consolidation. Is the AI compute boom about to shake out the small players?
caption:
Elon Musk says SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy NVIDIA GPUs arriving in early 2027.
He credited SpaceX's investment-grade rating and its Starlink and launch revenue.
He also warned that lenders have nearly stopped funding AI-only cloud companies, and that most of the 200+ "neoclouds" will not make it.

Is the AI compute boom about to wipe out the smaller players?

site_article.seo_title: SpaceX closes $40 billion GPU debt deal, Musk warns neoclouds
site_article.seo_description: Musk says SpaceX closed $40 billion in mostly callable debt to buy Nvidia GPUs arriving in 2027, and predicts a shakeout among 200+ AI cloud firms.
site_article.answer_summary: According to Elon Musk, SpaceX has closed $40 billion in mostly callable debt to buy Nvidia GPUs that arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027.

paragraphs.text: SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units, Elon Musk said in posts on X on Sunday, October 25, 2026. The chips come from Nvidia and are scheduled to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027, according to TipRanks and investingLive.

Musk described the package as mostly callable debt, meaning it can be repaid early under agreed terms. He wrote that the financing is "not a major factor this quarter." investingLive reported that it was not immediately clear whether investors had settled on pricing.

The Financial Times reported in early October that SpaceX was negotiating to borrow $40 billion for Nvidia chips, with roughly $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt, according to a summary by The Next Web. Apollo Global Management was expected to lead the sale, and Pimco was among the lenders in talks, according to that report.

Bloomberg later reported that a special purpose vehicle could keep the debt off SpaceX's balance sheet and that Goldman Sachs was leading talks with investors, according to investingLive. Musk credited SpaceX's investment-grade credit rating and its revenue from Starlink and rocket launches for the company's ability to raise the money.

The chips are meant for SpaceX's AI data centers. In August, Musk said the company would build those sites using only Nvidia hardware, and in September he said the Colossus 2 site could more than double its Nvidia chip count by December, The Next Web reported. SpaceX also rents out computing capacity, and Google reportedly agreed to pay $920 million a month for access to about 110,000 Nvidia GPUs.
AI is now SpaceX's largest business

The financing follows strong third-quarter results. SpaceX's AI unit is now its largest business, with third-quarter AI revenue up about ninefold to roughly $7.6 billion, investingLive reported. TipRanks put total third-quarter revenue at $14.58 billion, up 161% from a year earlier, and said Starlink ended September with 13.6 million consumer subscribers.

Spending is rising just as fast. Capital expenditure nearly tripled to $19.6 billion in the third quarter, and the company expects $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter as new computing sites open, according to TipRanks. SpaceX is also working with Tesla on Terafab, a chip plant that aims to produce a first test chip in May or June 2027.

Musk used the same posts to warn that debt markets have almost entirely stopped lending to companies that lack substantial revenue outside AI data centers. He wrote that the "200+ neoclouds" face "guppy-level death and consolidation" and added, "Some will make it through, but not many." He said SpaceX would not buy any of them, according to investingLive.

Neoclouds rent AI computing power to model developers and other customers, and many of them borrow to buy GPUs, TipRanks noted. investingLive named CoreWeave and Nebius as pure-play providers that could stay under pressure as investors question their access to debt.

The deal shows a widening split in how the AI build-out is financed. A borrower with an investment-grade rating and revenue from other businesses can still raise tens of billions of dollars, while companies whose only product is rented GPU capacity face a narrower path, if Musk's read of the credit market is right. For Nvidia, the order points to continued demand for its chips into 2027.

The next signal is the final pricing and structure of the SpaceX debt, along with any new financing announcements or deals from neocloud providers in the coming weeks, which will show whether lenders are as cautious as Musk describes.
